entries.title: Man, 16-year-old girl shot inside Gresham home
entries.summary: <p>A man and a 16-year-old girl were shot while inside a home in Gresham on Friday evening, Chicago police said.</p><p>Shortly before 7 p.m., a man, 49, was involved in a verbal altercation with someone he knew and was shot multiple times inside a home in the 7900 block of South Hermitage Avenue, police said.</p><p>The wounded man was transported to Advocate Christ Medical Center in critical condition, police said. A 16-year-old girl, also in the home, was struck by gunfire and taken to the same hospital in good condition.</p><p>A person of interest was questioned by police. Area detectives are investigating.</p>

entries.title: Lake View’s Kaleb Lovett owning the show in only his fourth year of football
entries.summary: <p>Kaleb Lovett didn’t play organized sports until his eighth-grade year and didn’t start tackle football until he got to high school.</p><p>Call the Lake View senior running back a fast learner.</p><p>Through the first six weeks of this season, Lovett ranked first in Illinois and 15th nationally with 1,153 rushing yards, according to the MaxPreps database. Even factoring in that not every school reports its stats, it’s a remarkable achievement for a player so new to the game.</p><p>And Lovett could be moving farther up the leaderboard after running 25 times for 296 yards and two touchdowns in the Wildcats’ epic 36-34 win over Von Steuben in five overtimes Thursday night.</p><p>How has Lovett done it? Credit his effort and an offensive line that returned all but one starter.</p><p>“I had to outwork everyone,” Lovett told the Sun-Times. “I had to do more than the regular load that everyone was taking on.”</p><p>He did, Lake View coach Kipp Duplechine confirmed.</p><p>“Coming from Louisiana, where I come from, there’s a lot of guys who run [4.4 or 4.5 in the 40-yard dash],” Duplechine said. “But work ethic-wise, he’s probably one of the top guys I’ve coached in a while. We had a banquet before the season, and I told everyone he’s the most improved player I’ve ever coached.</p><p>“Pound for pound, he’s one of the strongest guys. He only weighs like 165, but he squats with the linemen.”</p><p>Those linemen share a strong bond with Lovett, a 6-footer.</p><p>“I think the amount of appreciation he shows for us up front gives us a lot of motivation to block for him,” senior center Stephan Chi said.</p><p>Senior tackle Marc Schmidt saw Lovett’s breakout coming.</p><p>“Oh, yeah, I knew it from the start, from JV days when we were playing with each other and he would be running the ball or [playing] receiver,” Schmidt said. “He always made a statement for himself.”</p><p>Lovett didn’t get many carries last season because the Wildcats had senior Tyrone Townes, who earned All-City honorable mention and had a 300-yard rushing game against Public League North champ Curie. Lovett played mostly cornerback last year and is still doing that this season, along with a little wide receiver.</p><p>“He kind of reminds me of [Townes],” senior tackle Brent McMillin said. “His explosiveness is what really sticks out about him.”</p><p>Duplechine is reminded of former Saints quarterback and tight end Taysom Hill.</p><p>“[Lovett] was kind of like a Taysom Hill — plug him in at X, plug him in at receiver, cornerback, special teams,” he said. “But this year he just kind of locked in at tailback.”</p><p>Although Lake View is 6-1 and atop the White North at 4-0, attention isn’t always easy to come by for the Wildcats in general, or Lovett in particular. But Duplechine will be working his connections when the season is over to find a college home for his star.</p><p>“No one’s reached out yet, but it’s still very early,” Duplechine said. “We’re kind of overshadowed by Kenwood and Mount Carmel and all these other teams. But if you’re ranked No. 1 in the state in rushing and No. 15 in the country, someone’s going to call.</p><p>“He definitely has potential to play [NCAA Division 3 or 2], but I want to try to get him to a D1 school, at least an FCS school.”</p>

entries.title: Northwestern debuts Ryan Field, the most expensive college stadium ever
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports" target="_blank" >Northwestern’</a>s bold claim to the future of their sport — the most expensive college football stadium ever built — was baptized by the sounds of AC/DC’s “Thunderstruck” on Friday night.</p><p>As the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/10/01/limited-edition-willie-the-wildcat-bobblehead-commemorates-northwesterns-new-ryan-field" target="_blank" >Wildcats</a> prepared to run onto the field seconds before kickoff, the guitar licks bounced off the new concrete, old limestone and soccer-style canopy of the stadium. Players sprinted across the field and stopped in front of their new student section, the Wildcat Wall. Two thousand students stomped and kicked up an ear-splitting, Advil-reaching frenzy.</p><p>It was all so, well, not Northwestern. The Big Ten’s smallest, most demure fan base had never seen — or heard — anything like this. Moments after the Wildcats took the field, an NFL scout commented to no one in particular that it didn’t feel like a pro football stadium — it felt like an NBA arena, complete with throbbing music and flashy video.</p><p>Whether Northwestern can use the $875 million Ryan Field to its advantage remains to be seen. There were empty purple seats scattered throughout the 35,000-seat stadium — and many more covered by Penn State fans wearing white. Booster Pat Ryan’s dream stadium is unique to the Big Ten — it’s the smallest in the football-crazy league — if not the sport.</p><p>It was ready Friday because it had to be. When I took my dog for a walk eight hours before kickoff — I live down the street — employees were still screwing in streetlights and testing turnstiles with QR codes. Freshly planted flowers were being watered.</p><p>When it was clear the stadium wouldn’t be ready for the start of this season, serendipity brought Northwestern a worthy story line.</p><p>One hundred years ago to the day Friday, 18,000 fans watched the Purple beat South Dakota, 34-0, when they debuted their as-yet-unnamed $2 million stadium. Vic Gustafson scored a touchdown and then on the next play intercepted a pass and returned it for a touchdown as the first-half gun — back when they used one— sounded. Gustafson, who would go on to captain the Wildcats’ first Big Ten championship team the next year, had shared the backfield at Wheaton High School with none other than Red Grange.</p><p>A month later, the stadium was named after William Dyche, the former Evanston mayor and Northwestern vice president who had originally ordered the construction of wooden football bleachers in 1905. The Bears played there in 1970 when the NFL ruled that Wrigley Field was too small. A five-year contract to stay there was challenged by locals and eventually denied by the Big Ten. The team moved to Soldier Field the next year.</p><p>In 1997, the stadium was christened Ryan Field after the booster and longtime Northwestern Board of Trustees chair — who is the founder of AON and part-owner of the Bears — paid for a massive renovation. The stadium still felt old. In the 2008 Ernie Davis biopic “The Express,” it served as a stand-in for Syracuse’s Archbold Stadium, which had closed 30 years earlier.</p><p>The old stadium was torn down in February 2024. The Wildcats spent the interim two-and-a-half years splitting time between Martin Stadium on campus and Wrigley Field. The former, a soccer and lacrosse field steps from Lake Michigan, was fitted with expanded bleachers and food trucks. Playing at Wrigley Field in November allowed the Wildcats to avoid nastiest weather of the football season.</p><p>Construction at Central Street was met with consternation by some Evanston locals. It took a tiebreaking vote by Mayor Daniel Biss to approve the stadium plan, which included rezoning for concerts. In exchange, Northwestern agreed to contribute to various city funds and causes.Friday night, years of construction and a century of prelude produced Northwestern’s bold statement to the rest of the league.</p><p>Thunderstruck, indeed.<br></p>

entries.title: Sox postseason run has instilled pride in the South Side
entries.summary: <p>Sometimes baseball has no idea of the power it can wield. How it can ofttimes, depending on the circumstances that surround it, transcend a loss or a win, even one 21 years in the making.</p><p>“Sport has the power to change the world,” Nelson Mandela once said. “Sport can create hope where there was once only despair.”</p><p>Welcome to October. Welcome to the South Side, where despair has finally come to die.</p><p>Two seasons ago, the White Sox represented the bottomless and bottom-feeding “pit” of major-league baseball.</p><p>Today they come from a different place. Still the same side of town. Being in the American League Division Series, light-years ahead of anyone’s unrealistic thoughts, can do that to a community.</p><p>There’s the “know everything’s” claim that this is elation. That what skipper Will Venable likes to refer to as the “spirit of the team” belongs only to them. Thinking, possibly, that Munetaka Murakami’s champaign-soaked postgame meme-fest speaks only to the feeling of the team, short-sighting how an entire side of the third-largest city in America is drunk with him in that joy.</p><p>Not realizing what that team just accomplished exceeds way past baseball.</p><p>From inside Grandstand to outside on the street-level deck of Turtle’s. This ain’t just specific to 35th & Shields. This is how for a day — or seven — the people and patients walking about the Victory Center in Roseland can smile and how the kids in Adam Clayton Powell Jr. Paideia Academy in South Shore, until at least Wednesday night, can be infected with pride.</p><p>A feeling seeping inside Han Cha and Yunomi in the Stony Island Arts Bank to creeping outside Pressbox in Printer’s Row. In those eating dinner on a rainy Thursday in Ken’s on Western in Evergreen Park and getting an Italian beef or Nacho Supreme at the EZ Market outside O Block.</p><p>The Sox playing World Series-seeking baseball in October for the first time since they snatched the crown in 2005 to rewrite Chicago baseball history (a reminder: 11 years before the Cubs finally decided to shed their self-accepted “lovable losers” identity) is, as this newspaper put it, “what you don’t see in the box score.” Where we “understand how the Sox got here, what changed along the way and what the moment means to the people living it.”</p><p>It don’t rain in Southern California, but it rains bullets in the southern region of the Chi. Annie don’t live here because the sun never comes out tomorrow once you get south of Soldier Field and McCormick Place. Black being the Sox’ primary hex color because it goes with the funeral outfits so many of us on the South Side wear as customary uniforms based on the amount of services people believe we attend.</p><p>Antawun Carter and Jalil Sumerset are young diehard South Side residents and baseball savants who are finding ways to get tickets to the game Wednesday to be inside the Rate. Chance, Barack and Don C. searching their closets for postseason Sox pieces with tags still on them that they’ve been saving for just this moment. The Pope calling New Era for a new fitted.</p><p>It’s a hero’s journey that just happened to find baseball as its guide.</p><p>The first team in major-league history to lead every inning in a multiple-game postseason series is cute. But the depth of exactly what this is and reps remains far more profound than that. This isn’t about fans; this is about feelings. Feelings specific to an entire side of the city that has been continuously painted as those who are supposed to be numb to everything because of what our lives are supposed to be like on an everyday basis.</p><p>This win, this advance to the DS, this come-up before any type of come-up was thought to be logical, this culture Venable has created has infiltrated all blocks Commercial to Western, Lake Meadows to The Gardens, 18th and Blue Island Ave. to 119th and Cicero.</p><p>A less than 1% chance in April to make the postseason is the predicted market we walk around reminding ourselves of. Blurring the lines of the Sox with the lines of our lives. Happy to be trapped in their moment. Anything for the outside world to attach us to something different. To attach something positive inside of humanity to us.</p><p>For right now, for this momentary lapse in our perceived but hard to act like it doesn’t exist South Side societal anguish, the rain — at least in our minds — stops. The sun appears, if only for a week. The black we wear to match our Sox ’47s represents flyness, not funerals.</p><p>All championship teams have spirit. But until the Sox win one or even enter into that level of conversation, the true spirit of who they are, what they mean and how their impact resonates rests and breathes throughout the neighborhoods that have shouldered their burden for decades. Knowing the weight that 121 losses carries, knowing now what it feels like to have that weight lifted.</p><p>Like a roof that ain’t the ceiling. And the sun comes out. Tomorrow.</p>

entries.title: Brother Rice showcases its depth in Fenwick win
entries.summary: <p>Damari Thigpen had been taken off the return team earlier this season.</p><p>Brayden Parks is a four-star defensive lineman committed to Notre Dame.</p><p>Rocco Galasso began the year splitting time at quarterback with freshman Sam Holcomb before Holcomb won the starting job..</p><p>All of them flipped the script for No. 3 Brother Rice on Friday night as the Crusaders avoided a letdown after last week's rivalry win over Mount Carmel and pulled away to beat visiting Fenwick 42-21.</p><p>Thigpen ran a punt back 50 yards for a touchdown and almost did it again with a return to the Fenwick one-yard line. That set up the 310-pound Parks' second rushing TD of the game.</p><p>Galasso, meanwhile, stepped in with Holcomb sidelined by what coach Casey Quedenfeld called "a dental issue" and passed for 150 yards and a score for the Crusaders (5-2).</p><p>"We had to adjust based on our personnel with some of the injuries that we had and some of just misfortunes that we had going into this game," Quedenfeld said. "And you've just got to do the best that you can and move forward."</p><p>Thigpen returned one punt for a TD last season and has his sights set on the program career record of five.</p><p>"I've been working on it since last season but this year I haven't really been in a groove." Thigpen said.</p><p>Quedenfeld said the Crusaders changed returners this season after Thigpen had trouble fielding punts. But with the replacements out Friday, he resumed that role.</p><p>"Once we got close to the end of the regular season into the playoffs, he did a fantastic job returning punts and kicks," Quedenfeld said. "So hopefully he gets back into the groove like you just saw tonight. But in the beginning of the year, he was not doing what you saw tonight."</p><p>Neither was Parks, at least on offense. The consensus top-200 senior has teamed with five-star junior Kameron McGee to form an elite defensive line combo. They did their job on Friday, limiting Fenwick (4-3) to seven points over the first three quarters.</p><p>In the Week 6 win over Mount Carmel, Rice got McGee into the mix on offense with a key touchdown pass. On Friday, it was Parks' turn.</p><p>"It's definitely crazy that both of us get to just hop on the other side of the ball for a change," Parks said. "It just adds a dynamic or versatility to our offense."</p><p>Parks' first touchdown was part of a 28-0 run that turned a 7-3 first-quarter deficit into a 31-7 fourth-quarter lead.</p><p>"It's amazing, them trusting me with the ball, trusting me to punch it in," he said.</p><p>"We've been working on some different things to get guys involved," Quedenfeld said. "Whether it's Jack [McNamara] on the touchdown catch or Kameron catching the ball or different types of running backs and things like that."</p><p>McNamara's TD came on a short jump pass by Galasso, who was 13 of 22 passing with no interceptions. Jameson Davis added 118 rushing yards and a TD on 22 carries.</p><p>"Hopefully next week everyone's at full strength. whether it's running back, receiver, kick returner, punt returner, quarterback," Quedenfeld said.</p><p>Fenwick quarterback Myles Hill was 10 of 22 passing for 110 yards and one TD to Jake Thies. Hill and Thies, who had seven carries for 60 yards, also ran for touchdowns.<br></p>

entries.title: Mount Carmel QB Brady Cloherty ties his own school record with 7 TD passes against Providence
entries.summary: <p>Mount Carmel, the area’s heavily hyped, much-loved and hated football powerhouse, took its two losses on the chin this season in stoic fashion.</p><p>The Caravan didn’t make excuses, even though excuses were easily within grasp. Many fans might not even know how legitimate the excuses are.</p><p>Mount Carmel lost its starting quarterback, Ryder Startz, in the first half of the first game of the season. Then, a week later, defensive back Cullen Winters went down with an injury. Winters, a senior returning starter, was essentially the team's defensive play caller.</p><p>Senior Brady Cloherty stepped in for Startz and was immediately effective. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/01/high-school-football-scores-week-7" >Friday</a> against Providence, he took another step forward, throwing for 376 yards and seven touchdowns in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/09/27/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >No. 4 Caravan’s</a> 49-14 win against the No. 19 Celtics.</p><p>Mount Carmel's defense wasn’t as quick to adjust to missing a key player. But the Caravan is figuring it out. They shut out Providence in the second half.</p><p>“It has been tough without Cullen,” Mount Carmel defensive back Tavares Harrington, a Michigan recruit, said. “He’s a big-time player. We had to make some adjustments and took those two losses. But we are back now. We are getting in a groove, and he is coming back in a week or two, so we should be straight.”</p><p>Providence quarterback Dominic Vita connected with Hunter Long for a 93-yard touchdown with 4:52 left in the second quarter to tie the game at 14. It was all Mount Carmel from then on.</p><p>“We made some great halftime adjustments,” Caravan coach Jordan Lynch said. “It is what I’ve been looking for, to come out fast in the second half.”</p><p>Mount Carmel running back Nathan Samuels left with an injury after four carries.</p><p>“Coming in, we were going to run the ball a lot,” Cloherty said. “That changed this. So we went back to our nature—air raid—and it showed.”</p><p>Cloherty was 24-for-32 with no interceptions. He threw touchdown passes to Quentin Burrell, Jamarri Thompson, Marshaun Thornton and Danny Leyden and threw three touchdown passes to tight end Ty Kennedy, a junior transfer from Crown Point, Ind.</p><p>Kennedy has consistently become more involved in the offense.</p><p>“The receivers here are some of the best athletes in the country,” Kennedy said. “They’ve been helping me out with route running and pass catching.
